title: Grants Management — Awarding and Overseeing Financial Assistance
description: U.S. federal grants management blueprint: one mission with the outcomes it seeks and ways to measure them, eight capabilities from funding announcements through closeout with their reference requirements, example implementation patterns with their tradeoffs, and discovery question sets for grants results and for grants operations. It follows the Uniform Guidance in 2 CFR 200, and builds on Common Capabilities for case management, records, identity and access, data protection, and security logging.
jurisdictions: United States — federal agencies that award grants and cooperative agreements

sources.title: 2 CFR Part 200 — Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for Federal Awards
sources.note: The Uniform Guidance. Among much else: notices of funding opportunity posted on Grants.gov and generally open at least 60 days (§ 200.204), merit review (§ 200.205), review of applicants’ risk (§ 200.206), payment (§ 200.305), performance reporting no more often than quarterly and no less than annually (§ 200.329), remedies for noncompliance (§ 200.339), closeout (§ 200.344), the single audit for entities spending $1,000,000 or more a year (§ 200.501), and management decisions within six months (§ 200.521).

sources.title: 2 CFR Part 170 — Reporting Subaward and Executive Compensation Information
sources.note: The award term that has recipients report first-tier subawards of $30,000 or more no later than the end of the month after the subaward is made, under the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act.

sources.title: 2 CFR Part 25 — Unique Entity Identifier and System for Award Management
sources.note: Applicants register in SAM.gov and have a Unique Entity Identifier before they apply, with limited exceptions, and keep their registration current while they hold an award.

sources.title: 31 U.S.C. § 3352 — Estimates of improper payments and reports on actions to reduce improper payments
sources.note: Part of the Payment Integrity Information Act. Agencies review their programs at least once every 3 fiscal years for risk of significant improper payments, estimate them for programs at risk, and report the causes, corrective actions, and recoveries.

sources.title: Grants.gov
sources.note: Where agencies post funding opportunities and where most applicants find them and apply.

sources.title: SAM.gov — System for Award Management
sources.note: Entity registrations, exclusions, and responsibility and qualification records agencies check before an award. Since March 2025, recipients also report subawards here, after FSRS.gov was retired.

sources.title: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Bureau of the Fiscal Service — Do Not Pay
sources.note: A free service that helps agencies check a recipient’s identity and eligibility before making an award or a payment.

sources.title: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Bureau of the Fiscal Service — ASAP.gov
sources.note: The electronic system many agencies use to pay recipients, who draw down federal funds by requesting payments against the accounts agencies fund.

sources.title: USAspending.gov
sources.note: The official public source of federal spending data, including the financial assistance awards agencies report.

sources.title: Federal Audit Clearinghouse
sources.note: Run by GSA, the place where single audits of federal award recipients are submitted, and where agencies and the public review them.

sources.title: PaymentAccuracy.gov
sources.note: Agencies’ reported improper payment rates, amounts, causes, and recoveries, by program.

sources.title: Public Law 114-117 — Grants Oversight and New Efficiency Act (GONE Act)
sources.note: Had agencies report grant awards that had expired for 2 years or more without being closed out, and why, and then report which they closed. It shows how expired awards can pile up.

elements.title: Grants Management
elements.description: Award federal grants and cooperative agreements through fair, open competition to recipients able to manage them, pay them as their work needs funds, oversee how the money is used and what it achieves, resolve audit findings, close each award on time, and make the spending public.

elements.title: Funding is open to everyone eligible and fairly reviewed
elements.description: Funding opportunities are posted on Grants.gov with enough time to apply, generally at least 60 days, and applications are reviewed on their merits against criteria the notice describes.

measures.title: Funding opportunities open at least 60 days
measures.description: The share of the year’s funding opportunities that stayed open for applications at least 60 calendar days, the period the Uniform Guidance generally expects.

elements.title: Awards go to eligible recipients able to manage them
elements.description: Before each award, the agency checks the applicant’s eligibility and integrity records and the risk it poses, and sets conditions where the risk calls for them.

measures.title: Awards with a documented risk review
measures.description: The share of new awards whose file shows the eligibility, integrity, and risk checks done before the award, and any conditions they led to.

elements.title: Funds are paid as needed and used as the award allows
elements.description: Recipients get funds when their work needs them, and payments that shouldn’t have been made are prevented, or found and recovered.

measures.title: Improper payment rate
measures.description: For programs at risk of significant improper payments, the estimated share of payments that were improper or couldn’t be verified. Agencies report it each year, and PaymentAccuracy.gov publishes it.

measures.title: Improper payments recovered
measures.description: The amount of identified overpayments recovered, compared with the amount identified for recovery.

elements.title: Awards achieve what they were made for
elements.description: Recipients report their progress on schedule, the agency reviews it against the award’s goals, and problems are caught while there’s time to fix them.

measures.title: Performance reports received on time
measures.description: The share of required performance reports received by their due date, which is 30 days after a quarterly or semiannual period, or 90 days after an annual one.

elements.title: Audit findings are resolved promptly
elements.description: The agency decides what each audit finding about its awards requires within six months, and follows up until the recipient has corrected it.

measures.title: Management decisions within six months
measures.description: The share of audit findings about the agency’s awards that got a management decision within six months of the Federal Audit Clearinghouse accepting the audit report.

elements.title: Awards are closed out on time
elements.description: Recipients send their final reports within 120 days after the period of performance ends, and the agency closes each award within a year, returning unspent funds.

measures.title: Awards closed within a year
measures.description: The share of awards whose period of performance ended that were closed out within one year.

measures.title: Expired awards not yet closed
measures.description: The number of awards whose period of performance ended 2 years ago or more that are still open, and their undisbursed balances.

elements.title: The spending is open to view
elements.description: Each award, and recipients’ first-tier subawards, are reported for publication on USAspending.gov, so the public can see who receives federal funds and for what.

measures.title: Awards published on USAspending.gov
measures.description: The share of the agency’s financial assistance awards that appear on USAspending.gov with complete, accurate data, and how soon after the award they appear.

elements.title: Funding Opportunities & Applications
elements.description: Ability to announce each funding opportunity on Grants.gov with its goals, eligibility, criteria, and deadlines, receive applications through Grants.gov and any other allowed channel, and check each one for eligibility and completeness.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Some programs are formula or mandatory awards with no competition; the program’s statute and regulations set who can apply and how.

elements.title: Merit Review & Selection
elements.description: Ability to review discretionary applications on their merits against the written criteria the notice described, with reviewers free of conflicts of interest, and to record how each award decision was made.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Merit review applies to discretionary awards unless a statute says otherwise. Agencies set their own written standards for it.

elements.title: Risk Review & Award
elements.description: Ability to check each applicant’s eligibility, integrity, and risk before an award, using SAM.gov, Do Not Pay, and its financial stability, management systems, past performance, and audit findings, and to issue the award with its terms and any specific conditions.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Checks of responsibility and qualification records in SAM.gov are required when the federal share is expected to exceed the simplified acquisition threshold. An agency can still award to an applicant that falls short if conditions can address the risk.

elements.title: Payments to Recipients
elements.description: Ability to pay recipients in a way that keeps the time between payment and their spending short, by advance or by reimbursement, to review payment requests, and to hold or stop payments when the award’s terms call for it.
elements.applicabilityNotes: States are paid under their own Treasury agreements. Many agencies pay through ASAP.gov or another federal payment system.

elements.title: Monitoring & Performance Reporting
elements.description: Ability to collect recipients’ financial and performance reports on schedule, review them against the award’s goals and budget, monitor each award as its risk calls for, including site visits, and approve changes to awards.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Reports can be required no more often than quarterly and no less often than annually, unless specific conditions apply.

elements.title: Audit Resolution & Remedies
elements.description: Ability to find the single audit findings about the agency’s awards, decide what each one requires within six months, follow up until the recipient corrects it, and take remedies for noncompliance when needed, such as conditions, withheld payments, or termination.
elements.applicabilityNotes: A single audit is required of recipients that spend $1,000,000 or more a year in federal awards. Remedies must follow the steps the Uniform Guidance and the award’s terms set out.

elements.title: Closeout
elements.description: Ability to collect each recipient’s final reports within 120 days after the period of performance ends, reconcile payments and costs, return or deobligate unspent funds, and close the award within a year.
elements.applicabilityNotes: The agency can extend the time for final reports when the recipient asks and the reason supports it. Closing an award doesn’t end the right to disallow costs or collect amounts due.

elements.title: Award & Subaward Reporting
elements.description: Ability to report each financial assistance award for publication on USAspending.gov, keep the data accurate and complete, and see that recipients report their first-tier subawards in SAM.gov.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Some information is withheld from publication, such as details that would identify individual recipients.

elements.title: Post each funding opportunity on Grants.gov
elements.description: Post each notice of funding opportunity on Grants.gov with its goals, eligibility, review criteria, and deadlines, and keep it open at least 60 days unless a shorter period is justified.

elements.title: Check each application for eligibility and completeness
elements.description: Confirm each applicant is eligible, is registered in SAM.gov, and has included its Unique Entity Identifier, and that the application has what the notice asks for.

elements.title: Review applications against the published criteria
elements.description: Score each discretionary application against the criteria the notice described, following the agency’s written merit review standards, and keep the scores and comments.

elements.title: Keep reviewers free of conflicts of interest
elements.description: Have each reviewer disclose conflicts before seeing applications, and keep anyone with a conflict away from those applications.

elements.title: Check eligibility and integrity records before an award
elements.description: Check SAM.gov registration, exclusions, and, where required, responsibility and qualification records, and check Do Not Pay, before making an award.

elements.title: Document each applicant’s risk, and any conditions it calls for
elements.description: Record the review of the applicant’s financial stability, management systems, past performance, and audit findings, and any specific conditions added to the award because of them.

elements.title: Pay recipients as their work needs funds
elements.description: Keep advances to the recipient’s immediate cash needs, and pay reimbursement requests within 30 days unless the request looks improper.

elements.title: Review payment requests, and hold them when the terms call for it
elements.description: Look at payment requests against the award’s budget and status, and hold or stop payments under the award’s terms, such as when required reports are overdue.

elements.title: Collect financial and performance reports on schedule
elements.description: Set each award’s reporting schedule, collect its financial and performance reports by their due dates, and follow up on late ones.

elements.title: Monitor each award as its risk calls for
elements.description: Plan monitoring, such as desk reviews and site visits, by each award’s risk, review reports against the award’s goals and budget, and record what was found and done.

elements.title: Issue a management decision on each audit finding within six months
elements.description: Find the single audit findings about the agency’s awards in the Federal Audit Clearinghouse, and decide within six months of the audit report’s acceptance what each one requires.

elements.title: Follow up on corrective action, and take remedies when needed
elements.description: Track each recipient’s corrective action until it’s done, and when noncompliance isn’t corrected, take a remedy the Uniform Guidance allows, with notice to the recipient.

elements.title: Collect final reports within 120 days
elements.description: Remind recipients as the period of performance ends, collect their final financial and performance reports within 120 days, and decide requests for more time.

elements.title: Close each award within a year after it ends
elements.description: Reconcile payments and costs, settle any amounts due, deobligate what’s left, and complete closeout within one year after the period of performance ends.

elements.title: Report each award for publication on USAspending.gov
elements.description: Report each financial assistance award, and each change to it, for publication on USAspending.gov, and correct errors when they’re found.

elements.title: See that recipients report their subawards
elements.description: Include the subaward reporting term in each award, and follow up when recipients don’t report first-tier subawards of $30,000 or more in SAM.gov by the end of the month after they’re made.

elements.title: Grants Management
elements.description: An example architecture: one grants system that carries each award from the funding announcement through applications, merit review, risk checks, award, payments, monitoring, and closeout, with a portal where recipients apply, report, and ask for changes.

parts: Funding announcements prepared in the system and posted to Grants.gov
Applications received from Grants.gov, with eligibility and completeness checks
Reviewer assignments, conflict disclosures, and scoring against each notice’s criteria
Risk reviews and award documents with standard terms and any specific conditions
A recipient portal for reports, change requests, and closeout
Monitoring plans, site visit records, and audit findings for each award
The award data the agency reports to USAspending.gov
strengths: One record for each award, from announcement to closeout
Recipients have one place to apply, report, and ask for changes
fitsWhen: The agency runs grant programs with similar steps
Its current tools are spreadsheets, email, or an aging custom system
watchFor: Programs with unusual rules, such as formula awards, may not fit standard steps
Moving open awards from an old system mid-stream needs careful planning
Connections to the agency’s financial system and payment system often take the most work

ways.title: A grants management product
ways.description: A product made for grants, configured for the agency’s programs and run by the agency.
strengths: Built around the Uniform Guidance, so much of the process comes ready
fitsWhen: The agency runs several grant programs, with staff to administer a system
watchFor: Another product to buy, secure, and keep up

ways.title: A federal grants shared service
ways.description: A grants system another federal agency runs as a shared service, configured for the agency’s programs, under an agreement that sets the service, its costs, and who does what.
strengths: The provider keeps the system current with federal rules and systems
The agency doesn’t buy, host, or secure a system of its own
Recipients may already know the system from other agencies’ awards
fitsWhen: The agency’s grant programs are small or few
A shared service already serves programs like the agency’s
watchFor: Changes for the agency’s programs wait on the provider’s priorities
Getting the agency’s data out, for reporting or a later move, needs agreeing up front
Costs can grow with the number of awards and users

ways.title: The agency’s shared case platform
ways.description: Application and award records, their steps, and a recipient portal, built on the agency’s shared case platform.
strengths: Uses licenses, skills, and security approvals the agency already has
Grants work can share a platform with the agency’s other case work
fitsWhen: The agency already runs a platform like this, with people who configure it
Its programs are fairly simple, with few awards each
watchFor: Merit review, reporting forms, and the recipient portal often take more building than expected
Federal reporting, such as to USAspending.gov, has to be built and kept up
Rules change with the Uniform Guidance, and someone has to update the platform each time

elements.title: Grants Management Product
elements.description: An example architecture: a grants management product, configured for the agency’s programs, that carries each award from the funding announcement through applications, review, risk checks, award, payments, monitoring, and closeout, with a portal where recipients apply and report.

parts: Funding announcements prepared in the product and posted to Grants.gov
Applications received from Grants.gov, with eligibility and completeness checks
Reviewer assignments, conflict disclosures, and scoring against each notice’s criteria
Risk reviews and award documents with standard terms and any specific conditions
A recipient portal for reports, change requests, and closeout
Monitoring plans, site visit records, and audit findings for each award
The award data the agency reports to USAspending.gov
strengths: One record for each award, from announcement to closeout
Built around the Uniform Guidance, so much of the process comes ready
Recipients have one place to apply, report, and ask for changes
fitsWhen: The agency runs several grant programs with similar steps
Its current tools are spreadsheets, email, or an aging custom system
watchFor: Programs with unusual rules, such as formula awards, may not fit the product’s standard steps
Moving open awards from an old system mid-stream needs careful planning
Connections to the agency’s financial system and payment system often take the most work

elements.title: A Federal Grants Shared Service
elements.description: An example architecture: the agency uses a grants management system another federal agency runs as a shared service, configured for its programs, instead of running its own.

parts: The provider’s grants system, with the agency’s programs, forms, and workflows set up in it
An agreement that sets the service, its costs, and who does what
The provider’s connections to Grants.gov, payment systems, and USAspending.gov
The agency’s own staff for programs, awards, and monitoring
strengths: The provider keeps the system current with federal rules and systems
The agency doesn’t buy, host, or secure a system of its own
Recipients may already know the system from other agencies’ awards
fitsWhen: The agency’s grant programs are small or few
A shared service already serves programs like the agency’s
watchFor: Changes for the agency’s programs wait on the provider’s priorities
Getting the agency’s data out, for reporting or a later move, needs agreeing up front
Costs can grow with the number of awards and users

elements.title: Grants on the Agency’s Shared Platform
elements.description: An example architecture: grants management built on the agency’s shared case platform, with each application and award as a record that moves through review, award, monitoring, and closeout, and a portal for recipients.

parts: Application and award records, with their status, dates, amounts, and documents
Steps and approvals for review, risk checks, award, and closeout
A recipient portal for reports and change requests
A connection to Grants.gov for announcements and applications
Reports on each program’s awards, monitoring, and closeout
strengths: Uses licenses, skills, and security approvals the agency already has
Grants work can share a platform with the agency’s other case work
Each program can change its steps by configuration
fitsWhen: The agency already runs a platform like this, with people who configure it
Its programs are fairly simple, with few awards each
watchFor: Merit review, reporting forms, and the recipient portal often take more building than expected
Federal reporting, such as to USAspending.gov, has to be built and kept up
Rules change with the Uniform Guidance, and someone has to update the platform each time

elements.title: Applications from Grants.gov by System-to-System Connection
elements.description: An example architecture: the agency’s grants system connects to Grants.gov’s system-to-system service, so funding opportunities are posted and applications arrive as records with their forms and attachments, instead of being downloaded by hand.

parts: A connection in the agency’s grants system to Grants.gov’s system-to-system service
Posting of funding opportunities from the grants system
Retrieval of each application, with its forms and attachments, into an application record
Status sent back to Grants.gov, so applicants can see where their application is
Monitoring for applications that fail to arrive
strengths: No downloading and retyping of applications
Applicants use the site most of them already know
fitsWhen: The agency runs its own grants system, product or built
It gets many applications for each opportunity
watchFor: Changes to Grants.gov’s forms and service need following
Applications that fail to arrive must be noticed before the deadline passes

ways.title: A connection to Grants.gov’s system-to-system service

elements.title: Payments through Treasury’s ASAP.gov
elements.description: An example architecture: the agency enrolls each recipient in ASAP.gov, funds an account for each award from its financial system, and recipients draw down funds as they need them, within the controls the agency sets.

parts: Recipient enrollment in ASAP.gov, with their banking details kept by Treasury
An account for each award, funded from the agency’s financial system as the award is obligated
Controls the agency sets, such as review of requests over a set amount
Drawdown data sent back to the agency’s financial and grants systems
Suspension of an account when the award’s terms call for it
strengths: Treasury runs the payment system and holds recipients’ banking details
Recipients draw funds as they need them, which keeps the time before they spend short
Many recipients already use it for other agencies’ awards
fitsWhen: The agency pays recipients by advance or drawdown
Its financial system can send obligations to ASAP.gov
watchFor: Drawdown data has to be reconciled with the agency’s financial and grants records
Controls on requests need setting for each award, or large drawdowns go through unchecked

elements.title: Grant Risk Analytics
elements.description: An example architecture: an analytics workspace that brings together SAM.gov and Do Not Pay results, single audit findings, past performance, and drawdown patterns for each applicant and recipient, and suggests where risk reviews and monitoring should look first, with the reasons.

parts: Regular feeds from SAM.gov, Do Not Pay, the Federal Audit Clearinghouse, and the agency’s grants and payment systems
A risk profile for each applicant and recipient, with the facts behind it
Flags for patterns worth a closer look, such as late reports or large drawdowns near an award’s end
Suggested monitoring priorities for the year, which program staff accept or change
A record of what was flagged, what staff decided, and what came of it
strengths: Risk reviews start from the facts already known about an applicant
Monitoring goes where the risk is, instead of being spread evenly
Results show which risk signals are worth keeping
fitsWhen: The agency makes many awards, too many to monitor each one closely
Its grants and payment data can be brought together regularly
watchFor: A flag isn’t a finding, so staff decide each award, condition, and monitoring step
Risk scores can be unfair to new or small applicants with little history, so how they’re used needs care
Combining data sets may need agreements, and privacy rules apply to information about individuals

elements.title: Award Data to USAspending.gov from the Grants System
elements.description: An example architecture: the grants system produces the agency’s financial assistance award data on a schedule, checks it against the agency’s financial records, and submits it for publication on USAspending.gov, with errors sent back to the staff who can fix them.

parts: An extract of new awards and changes from the grants system, on a schedule
Checks against the agency’s financial records before each submission
Submission for publication on USAspending.gov, with the results recorded
A list of errors and missing data, sent to the staff who own each award
A list of awards whose recipients haven’t reported subawards
strengths: Award data is reported on time without a manual scramble
Errors are found and fixed at the source
fitsWhen: The agency’s grants system holds the award data, but reporting is manual today
watchFor: The data standard changes from time to time, and the extract has to follow
Fixes made in the submission instead of the grants system come back next time

ways.title: Scheduled submissions from the grants system

elements.title: Grants Management North Star
elements.description: The long-term architecture this library recommends for a grants office: one grants system that carries each award from the funding announcement to closeout, connected to Grants.gov, ASAP.gov, and USAspending.gov, with the same SAM.gov checks for every applicant and risk analytics that point monitoring at the highest risks.

principles: Each award is one record from the funding announcement to closeout
Applications arrive from Grants.gov, and award data goes to USAspending.gov, without retyping
Recipients have one place to apply, report, and ask for changes
Every applicant gets the same SAM.gov checks, recorded with the award decision
Payments go through Treasury, against accounts set up from each award
Analytics point monitoring at the highest risks, and staff decide
watchFor: Programs with unusual rules, such as formula awards, may need steps of their own
When the agency’s programs are few or small, a federal shared service can take the product’s place

Flags unusual drawdowns, such as large requests near the end of an award, for a closer look.

Each finding tracked as its own case, from management decision to closure.
Where the system produces the agency’s award submission. Checking it and following up on subaward reporting often happen outside it.
The award records and steps are the shared platform, set up for grants.
Applications arrive from Grants.gov through the system’s connection.
Awards and their amounts feed the payment system’s accounts.
Risk scores show in the system’s review and monitoring screens.
Drawdown patterns feed the risk analytics.
The same SAM.gov checks feed each applicant’s and recipient’s risk profile.
Staff sign in through the agency, with roles the grants office administers.
Posts each opportunity and brings each application into the grants system.
A product made for grants, configured for the agency’s programs, so the Uniform Guidance’s steps come ready.
Where staff and reviewers draft and collaborate, with records and sensitivity labels applied.
The grants system checks each applicant’s registration and exclusions before award.
Accounts set up from each award in the grants system, with drawdowns reported back.
The grants system’s award records, checked against the financial system and submitted on schedule.
